> Also, CI seems to fail due to some GDExtension stuff that I am unfamiliar with, I'd appreciate a pointer to the fix.

The failures are because you reordered some enums around (specifically the Light3D `PARAM_*` enum), which breaks compatibility with existing projects. Make sure you only add new values at the end; never move existing values or remove them.

I believe that, for now, to provide some level of mobile support and compatibility, area lights will only be usable through lightmap baking. I don't think anyone has the time to research and implement real-time area lights with acceptable performance, especially on mobile devices.

@LiveTrower I would see no reason, why area lights shouldn't work on mobile, or in compatibility. In fact, they should work now (just need to fix up the shadows in compat).

I expect area lights will perform somewhat OK on Mobile and Compatibility with shadows disabled, but I would avoid enabling shadows for them (but this applies to all light types in general when working with mobile/low-end platforms). PCSS-style variable penumbra shadows don't work in Mobile and Compatibility anyway, so the Light3D Size property will only affect the size of the specular lobe and the light's diffuse appearance anyway.

Last time I checked, there are some remnants of PCSS-style shadows in the Mobile renderer, but these were meant to be removed due to performance concerns: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/55882

@Calinou I agree, lighting computations are just mildly more complex than for point lights. They require two texture lookups, but the textures are constant, so should not be an issue even in Compatibility. Shadows in Compatibility don't work anyways since there is no dual paraboloid shadow pass, so I disabled them now. For the mobile renderer, shadows do work, but as you say, variable penumbra doesn't. Would you rather note that in documentation, or disable shadows entirely there?

I don't know if it's standard terminology, but I would avoid naming it **AreaLight3D** as "Area" in Godot usually refers to the entirely separate concept in the physics engine.

AreaLight is a common term to refer to this kind of lights

https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/lights/light_object.html#area-light

Apart from specifying the type of light precisely (RectLight, TubeLight, DiskLight, ...), I would like to highlight that "area light" is the used term not only in applications but also across scientific literature, so for the sake of later extensibility and for users to easily find the node, it makes the most sense to just call it `AreaLight3D`.

I was wondering if it's worth adding other shapes of LTC besides the rectangle one, and I think the only one that would be worthwhile is the tube or line shape since many real-world light sources have that form. The other shapes, like a disk, are very rare to see, and the sphere shape can be more or less created with an omnilight by increasing its 'size' property, but it looks more like an egg than a sphere. Is this normal? Also mention that with the roughness at 0 the reflection glitches. But I also saw that you can create a line and sphere shapes without it being an area light. In fact, Unreal Engine provides [this option](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/point-lights-in-unreal-engine) in its point light as does Wicked Engine. This could be easier to implement and maintain, as a big obstacle with LTC area lights is that their code isn't reusable. Adding another shape can mean having to create a different implementation for each shape and taking into account effects such as GI, subsurface scattering, anisotropy, clearcoat, toon shading, etc. This can complicate maintaining so many versions of area lights, and I'm not sure if the LUTs can be reused, since from what I've seen, you also have to generate a different LUT for each shading effect.

I was asked
1. does it work with volumetric fog
2. does it work with SSR

> 1. does it work with volumetric fog

It doesn't work with volumetric fog yet, but it may give acceptable results to treat it as a spot light there. The same applies to many other PBR effects, possibly even VoxelGI/SDFGI (it should be possible to have an accurate area light implementation in LightmapGI).

> 2. does it work with SSR

It should work with SSR already, since SSR purely relies on screen-space information and doesn't need to be modified to work with specific light types. SSR does not perform the rendering of specular lobes, but it will reflect specular lobes that appear on surfaces that are reflected in SSR.

@Calinou Thanks for testing, I confused a conditional operator; fixed. 
One thing I forgot to mention is that right now, the light needs to have a minimum range of 1.0m to affect fog at all. Otherwise we get intense flickering at the surface of the light.

As to why the light is weak compared to the point light: I divided the solid angle by 2*PI to give a ratio of how much of the hemisphere is covered by the light. Physically, this should make sense. But, if we remove this division, we get a light that is stronger and more similar in its intensity to the point light at a size of `(1,1)`. That change would also make the area light much stronger compared to point lights when it has a large size.

Btw the energy of an area light is interpreted as illuminance (luminous power per unit area), i.e. if you increase the size of the light, the illumination of the scene is stronger. A different approach would be to interpret the energy parameter as power, i.e. divide it by the area before using it in lighting calculations.

PS: Did you look at [physical light units](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/3d/physical_light_and_camera_units.html) in the context of AreaLight3D? I'm not sure what units are established standards for them (lumen, lux, nit?).

So, this is where things get messy... 

From my quick research, it seems area lights are unsupported in the common 3D formats. I found no existing or planned extension for area lights in the glTF format (as the name suggests, `KHR_lights_punctual` cares only about point/spot lights). fbx apparently knows about area lights, but ignores the shape and intensity. Blender, of course, stores area lights with an enum for its shape, and a size field (https://docs.blender.org/api/current/bpy.types.AreaLight.html). 

I did also look at physical light units. Blender stores all lights in terms of radiant power (`W` = Watts), which is non-standard. 
When exporting Blender point lights to glTF in "Standard" units, watts are converted to candela (`= lm/sr`), with the conversion `S / (4π) * 683`, see https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/73624#issuecomment-1745578491.
The energy of area lights can be represented either in lumens (luminous power), or nits (luminance, cd/m<sup>2</sup>), depending on whether a change in size should affect energy output. So, the Blender lights would be converted to lumens with the conversion `S * 683`, but I remember when matching light intensities between Blender and Gotot empirically, I had a very different conversion rate. 
As for other engines, Unity allows selecting between lumens and nits, with lumens being the default. If nits are selected, changes in size do affect energy output. Unreal Engine allows selecting between candelas and lumens, with candelas being the default (1cd=3,14 lm, which for my understanding does not make much sense, since the solid angle of a hemisphere is 2π sr, so it should be 1cd = 6,28lm for an area light?). In any case, changing size does not affect energy output. Both engines also support EV. 

-> It seems, that the more easily understood unit is more likely lumens and that size should not affect energy output. I should be able to adjust for that when I have time. I should highlight that for spotlights, on the other hand, the cone angle does affect the energy output, and the unit of the parameter would thus actually be something like lm/sr, but the way it is probably makes it more intuitive.

To shed some light on this in short: In Godot, for point lights, we calculate shadows with one shadow map, and use PCSS to get a soft (but not actually physically accurate) penumbra. This penumbra is larger the bigger the `size` parameter. However, point lights also change the specular reflection when the size parameter changes. In combination those two effects give the illusion that the light has a non-zero size.
Apart from ray-tracing, there are not really any feasible ways to calculate accurate shadows for lights with a non-zero size (I did many experiments with combining multiple shadow maps, but the resulting shadows were incorrectly shaped at best, and had abysmal performance at worst). So for area lights, we also use the PCSS method, which is controlled by the 'size' parameter. 
I agree that this is confusing, but also, that we shouldn't make the light size controlled by the area size, since it has significant performance implications in PCSS, and has very different limits than the area size.
In my book, point lights could have two separate size parameters, one for 'size for illumination', and one 'size for soft shadows'. Area lights then would only have a 'size for soft shadows' parameter.

So.... I added the checkbox for the normalization now. I also realized while investigating the fog issue, that attenuation was calculated incorreclty. Just so you know, area lights (calculated with LTC or with solid angle) already attenuate with the inverse square by default. I used to multiply by the omni attenuation to the closest point, so we used to have a cubic attenuation when the attenuation value was set to `1.0`, which is why the values were so different to omni lights. I fixed this by calling the omni attenuation function with `attenuation - 2.0`. This means, that with a default value of 1.0 for attenuation, we actually first calculate area lights with inverse square attenuation, and then multiply by distance, such that we sort of get linear attenuation. There was also an unnecessary clamping that inhibited negative attenuation having an effect, which I removed as well. Now as you can see in the images below, the intensities are now closely matched. 

The omni/spot lights (left) and area lights (right) below always use the same energy values.

![AreaLightAttenuation (1)](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8e7c851e-5750-458e-8fe9-5ba6115c13c3)

![LightEffects](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5e8e35c1-d9a5-424a-9b6c-8f65cbd56da4)

For fog, where I use the solid angle calculation, I actually also had to include a normalization factor of `7.801015826317776`. This magic number is calculated as `1/s`, where `s` is the solid angle of a quad with size `(1,1)` at a distance of `1` divided by `2*pi`.

@Calinou Implemented the custom light section, in Forward/Mobile and Compat.
In that case, LTC calculations are not done, and it does not give the user any way to obtain the light's extents, (or texture if that will be implemented), since ther are no suitable built-ins for that, so the usability of the custom light function might feel more limited for area lights. So, the `ATTENUATION` parameter is the only thing that accounts for the shape of the light.

Added built-ins for using area lights in custom shaders. Here's a list: - `bool LIGHT_IS_AREA`: whether the light is an area light or not - `float LIGHT_AREA_DIFFUSE`: if light is an area light, it is the diffuse (Lambertian) contribution of the light, otherwise it's 1.0 - `float LIGHT_AREA_SPECULAR`: if light is an area light, it is the specular (GGX) contribution of the light, otherwise it's 1.0 - `vec3 LIGHT_AREA_DIFFUSE_TEX_COLOR`: if light is an area light and has a texture assigned (coming soon), it is the color sampled on the texture for the diffuse contribution, otherwise it's vec3(1.0) - `vec3 LIGHT_AREA_SPECULAR_TEX_COLOR `: if light is an area light and has a texture assigned (coming soon), it is the color sampled on the texture for the specular contribution, otherwise it's vec3(1.0) And a playground project: [AreaLightCustomShader.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23939922/AreaLightCustomShader.zip)

You need to subdivide meshes enough so that the dual parabolid distortion can do its job (similar to OmniLight3D shadows that use the dual parabolid shadow mode). This is required for shadow maps to be accurate. Baked LightmapGI shadows don't have this limitation, and raytraced shadows wouldn't have this limitation if implemented in the future.

For most BoxMeshes, using 5 subdivision levels on all axes should suffice (but you'll need more for particularly large boxes).
